blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class XI, while studying Analytical Geometry in two
dimensions, and the introduction to three dimensional
geometry, we confined to the Cartesian methods only. In
the previous chapter of this book, we have studied some
basic concepts of vectors. We will now use vector algebra
to three dimensional geometry. The purpose of this
approach to 3-dimensional geometry is that it makes the
study simple and elegant*.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we shall study the direction cosines
and direction ratios of a line joining two points and also
discuss about the equations of lines and planes in space
under different conditions, angle between two lines, two
planes, a line and a plane, shortest distance between two
skew lines and distance of a point from a plane. Most of
the above results are obtained in vector form. Nevertheless, we shall also translate
these results in the Cartesian form which, at times, presents a more clear geometric
and analytic picture of the situation.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.2 Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios of a Line

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Chapter 10, recall that if a directed line L passing through the origin makes
angles $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ with $x$, $y$ and $z$-axes, respectively, called direction angles, then cosine
of these angles, namely, $\cos \alpha$, $\cos \beta$ and $\cos \gamma$ are called direction cosines of the
directed line L.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we reverse the direction of L, then the direction angles are replaced by their supplements,
i.e., $\pi - \alpha$, $\pi - \beta$ and $\pi - \gamma$. Thus, the signs of the direction cosines are reversed.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text:
* For various activities in three dimensional geometry, one may refer to the Book
“A Hand Book for designing Mathematics Laboratory in Schools”, NCERT, 2005

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that a given line in space can be extended in two opposite directions and so it
has two sets of direction cosines. In order to have a unique set of direction cosines for
a given line in space, we must take the given line as a directed line. These unique
direction cosines are denoted by $l$, $m$ and $n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$Remark$ If the given line in space does not pass through the origin, then, in order to find
its direction cosines, we draw a line through the origin and parallel to the given line.
Now take one of the directed lines from the origin and find its direction cosines as two
parallel line have same set of direction cosines.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Any three numbers which are proportional to the direction cosines of a line are
called the *direction ratios* of the line. If $l$, $m$, $n$ are direction cosines and $a$, $b$, $c$ are
direction ratios of a line, then $a = \lambda l$, $b = \lambda m$ and $c = \lambda n$, for any nonzero $\lambda \in \mathbf{R}$.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: Some authors also call direction ratios as direction numbers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $a, b, c$ be direction ratios of a line and let $l, m$ and $n$ be the direction cosines
$(d.c's)$ of the line. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\frac{l}{a} = \frac{m}{b} = \frac{n}{c} = k$ (say), $k$ being a constant.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $l = ak, m = bk, n = ck$ ... (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
But $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$
Therefore $k^2 (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = 1$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$k = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, from (1), the $d.c.$'s of the line are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$l = \pm \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}, m = \pm \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}, n = \pm \frac{c}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where, depending on the desired sign of $k$, either a positive or a negative sign is to be
taken for $l$, $m$ and $n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For any line, if $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of a line, then $ka, kb, kc; k \neq 0$ is also a
set of direction ratios. So, any two sets of direction ratios of a line are also proportional.
Also, for any line there are infinitely many sets of direction ratios.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 11.2.1 Direction cosines of a line passing through two points

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since one and only one line passes through two given points, we can determine the
direction cosines of a line passing through the given points $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$
as follows (Fig 11.2 (a)).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $l, m, n$ be the direction cosines of the line PQ and let it makes angles $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$
with the $x, y$ and $z$-axis, respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw perpendiculars from P and Q to XY-plane to meet at R and S. Draw a
perpendicular from P to QS to meet at N. Now, in right angle triangle PNQ, $\angle PQN = \gamma$
(Fig 11.2 (b).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\cos \gamma = \frac{\text{NQ}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{z_2 - z_1}{\text{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly $\cos \alpha = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{\text{PQ}}$ and $\cos \beta = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{\text{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Hence, the direction cosines of the line segment joining the points $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and
$Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{x_2 - x_1}{\text{PQ}} , \frac{y_2 - y_1}{\text{PQ}} , \frac{z_2 - z_1}{\text{PQ}} $$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note The direction ratios of the line segment joining $\mathrm{P}(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x_2, y_2, z_2)$
may be taken as
$$x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1, z_2 - z_1 \text{ or } x_1 - x_2, y_1 - y_2, z_1 - z_2$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Example 1** If a line makes angle $90^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ with the positive direction of $x$, $y$ and
$z$-axis respectively, find its direction cosines.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Let the $d.c.$'s of the lines be $l, m, n$. Then $l = \cos 90^0 = 0, m = \cos 60^0 = \frac{1}{2}$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$n = \cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 If a line has direction ratios $2, -1, -2$, determine its direction cosines.

Solution Direction cosines are

$$\frac{2}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + (-2)^2}}, \frac{-1}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + (-2)^2}}, \frac{-2}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + (-2)^2}}$$

or $$\frac{2}{3}, \frac{-1}{3}, \frac{-2}{3}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 Find the direction cosines of the line passing through the two points
$(-2, 4, -5)$ and $(1, 2, 3)$.
Solution We know the direction cosines of the line passing through two points
$P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are given by

$$\frac{x_2 - x_1}{PQ}, \frac{y_2 - y_1}{PQ}, \frac{z_2 - z_1}{PQ}$$

where $$PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$$

Here $P$ is $(-2, 4, -5)$ and $Q$ is $(1, 2, 3)$.
So $$PQ = \sqrt{(1 - (-2))^2 + (2 - 4)^2 + (3 - (-5))^2} = \sqrt{77}$$

Thus, the direction cosines of the line joining two points is

$$\frac{3}{\sqrt{77}}, \frac{-2}{\sqrt{77}}, \frac{8}{\sqrt{77}}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 4 Find the direction cosines of $x$, $y$ and $z$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution** The $x$-axis makes angles $0^{\circ}$, $90^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$ respectively with $x$, $y$ and $z$-axis.
Therefore, the direction cosines of $x$-axis are $\cos 0^{\circ}$, $\cos 90^{\circ}$, $\cos 90^{\circ}$ i.e., 1,0,0.
Similarly, direction cosines of $y$-axis and $z$-axis are 0, 1, 0 and 0, 0, 1 respectively.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 Show that the points A ($2, 3, - 4$), B ($1, - 2, 3$) and C ($3, 8, - 11$) are
collinear.

Solution Direction ratios of line joining A and B are
$1 - 2, - 2 - 3, 3 + 4$ i.e., $- 1, - 5, 7$.
The direction ratios of line joining B and C are
$3 - 1, 8 + 2, - 11 - 3$, i.e., $2, 10, - 14$.
It is clear that direction ratios of AB and BC are proportional, hence, AB is parallel
to BC. But point B is common to both AB and BC. Therefore, A, B, C are
collinear points.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: EXERCISE 11.1

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:

direction cosines.
2. Find the direction cosines of a line which makes equal angles with the coordinate
axes.
3. If a line has the direction ratios $-18, 12, -4$, then what are its direction cosines ?
4. Show that the points $(2, 3, 4), (-1, -2, 1), (5, 8, 7)$ are collinear.
5. Find the direction cosines of the sides of the triangle whose vertices are

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.3 Equation of a Line in Space

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have studied equation of lines in two dimensions in Class XI, we shall now study
the vector and cartesian equations of a line in space.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A line is uniquely determined if

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
A line is uniquely determined if
(i) it passes through a given point and has given direction, or
(ii) it passes through two given points.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 11.3.1 Equation of a line through a given point and parallel to $\vec{a}$ given vector $\vec{b}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $\vec{a}$ be the position vector of the given point A with respect to the origin O of the
rectangular coordinate system. Let $l$ be the line which passes through the point A and
is parallel to a given vector $\vec{b}$. Let $\vec{r}$ be the position vector of an arbitrary point P on the
line (Fig 11.3).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Then $\overline{\mathrm{AP}}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}$, i.e.,
$\overline{\mathrm{AP}} = \lambda \vec{b}$, where $\lambda$ is some real number.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
But $\overline{\mathrm{AP}} = \overline{\mathrm{OP}} - \overline{\mathrm{OA}}$
i.e. $\lambda \vec{b} = \vec{r} - \vec{a}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Conversely, for each value of the
parameter $\lambda$, this equation gives the position
vector of a point P on the line. Hence, the
vector equation of the line is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{r} = \vec{a} + \text{''} \vec{b} \tag{1} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\textit{Remark}$ If $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$, then $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the line and conversely,
if $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of a line, then $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$ will be the parallel to
the line. Here, $b$ should not be confused with $|\vec{b}|$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Derivation of cartesian form from vector form

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let the coordinates of the given point A be $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and the direction ratios of
the line be $a, b, c$. Consider the coordinates of any point P be $(x, y, z)$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\bar{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}; \bar{a} = x_1 \hat{i} + y_1 \hat{j} + z_1 \hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\bar{b} = a \hat{i} + b \hat{j} + c \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting these values in (1) and equating the coefficients of $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$x = x_1 + \lambda a; \ y = y_1 + \lambda b; \ z = z_1 + \lambda c \qquad \dots (2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
These are parametric equations of the line. Eliminating the parameter $\lambda$ from (2),
we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c} \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is the Cartesian equation of the line.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
If $l, m, n$ are the direction cosines of the line, the equation of the line is

$$\frac{x - x_1}{l} = \frac{y - y_1}{m} = \frac{z - z_1}{n}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 Find the vector and the Cartesian equations of the line through the point
$(5, 2, -4)$ and which is parallel to the vector $3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}$.
Solution We have
$$\vec{a} = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k} \text{ and } \vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the vector equation of the line is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{r} = 5 \hat{i} + 2 \hat{j} - 4 \hat{k} + \lambda ( 3 \hat{i} + 2 \hat{j} - 8 \hat{k} ) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, $\vec{r}$ is the position vector of any point $\mathrm{P}(x, y, z)$ on the line.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, $x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k} = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k} + \lambda ( 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 8\hat{k} )$
$= (5 + 3\lambda)\hat{i} + (2 + 2\lambda)\hat{j} + (-4 - 8\lambda)\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Eliminating $\lambda$, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the equation of the line in Cartesian form.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.5 Shortest Distance between Two Lines

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If two lines in space intersect at a point,
then the shortest distance between them is
zero. Also, if two lines in space are parallel,
then the shortest distance between them
will be the perpendicular distance, i.e. the
length of the perpendicular drawn from a
point on one line onto the other line.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Further, in a space, there are lines which
are neither intersecting nor parallel. In fact,
such pair of lines are *non coplanar* and
are called *skew lines*. For example, let us
consider a room of size 1, 3, 2 units along
$x, y$ and $z$-axes respectively Fig 11.5.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The line GE that goes diagonally across the ceiling and the line DB passes through
one corner of the ceiling directly above A and goes diagonally down the wall. These
lines are skew because they are not parallel and also never meet.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
By the shortest distance between two lines we mean the join of a point in one line
with one point on the other line so that the length of the segment so obtained is the
smallest.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For skew lines, the line of the shortest distance will be perpendicular to both
the lines.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 11.5.1 Distance between two skew lines

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We now determine the shortest distance between two skew lines in the following way:
Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be two skew lines with equations (Fig. 11.6)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}_1 \quad \dots (1) $$

and $$ \vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}_2 \quad \dots (2) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Take any point S on $l_1$ with position vector $\vec{a}_1$ and T on $l_2$, with position vector $\vec{a}_2$.
Then the magnitude of the shortest distance vector
will be equal to that of the projection of ST along the
direction of the line of shortest distance (See 10.6.2).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $\overrightarrow{\text{PQ}}$ is the shortest distance vector between $l_1$
and $l_2$, then it being perpendicular to both $\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{b}_2$,
the unit vector $\hat{n}$ along $\overrightarrow{\text{PQ}}$ would therefore be

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|} \qquad \dots (3) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Then $\overline{\text{PQ}} = d \hat{n}$
where, $d$ is the magnitude of the shortest distance vector. Let $\theta$ be the angle between
$\overline{\text{ST}}$ and $\overline{\text{PQ}}$. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$PQ = ST |\cos \theta|$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
But
$$\cos \theta = \left| \frac{\overline{\text{PQ}} \cdot \overline{\text{ST}}}{\left| \overline{\text{PQ}} \right| \left| \overline{\text{ST}} \right|} \right|$$
$$= \left| \frac{d \hat{n} \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{d \text{ ST}} \right| \quad (\text{since } \overline{\text{ST}} = \vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)$$
$$= \left| \frac{(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{\text{ST} \left| \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 \right|} \right| \quad [\text{From (3)}]$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the required shortest distance is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$d = \mathrm{PQ} = \mathrm{ST} |\cos \theta|$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$d = \left| \frac{(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 \times \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|} \right|$$

blocks.text: Cartesian form

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 11.5.2 Distance between parallel lines

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel, then they are coplanar. Let the lines be given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \begin{aligned} \bar{r} &= \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b} & ... (1) \\ \text{and} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \vec{r} &= \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b} & ... (2) \end{aligned} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where, $\vec{\text{a}}_1$ is the position vector of a point S on $l_1$ and $\vec{\text{a}}_2$
is the position vector of a point T on $l_2$ Fig 11.7.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As $l_1, l_2$ are coplanar, if the foot of the perpendicular
from T on the line $l_1$ is P, then the distance between the
lines $l_1$ and $l_2 = |\text{TP}|$.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 11.7

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{ST}}$ and $\vec{b}$.
Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{b} \times \overrightarrow{\text{ST}} = (|\vec{b}||\overrightarrow{\text{ST}}|\sin \theta)\hat{n} ... \tag{3} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane of the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: But $\overline{\text{ST}} = \vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, from (3), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = \vec{b} |\text{PT } \hat{n} \quad (\text{since PT = ST } \sin \theta)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)| = |\vec{b}| \text{ PT} \cdot 1 \quad (\text{as } |\hat{n}| = 1)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the distance between the given parallel lines is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$d = |\overline{\mathbf{P}\mathbf{T}}| = \left| \frac{\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}|} \right|$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 Find the shortest distance between the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ whose vector
equations are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda ( 2 \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k} ) \quad ... (1) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\vec{r} = 2 \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu (3 \hat{i} - 5 \hat{j} + 2 \hat{k}) \quad \dots (2)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Comparing (1) and (2) with $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{\text{r}} = \vec{\text{a}}_2 + \mu \vec{\text{b}}_2$ respectively,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
we get $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \bar{a}_1 = \hat{i} + \hat{j} \text{ , } \bar{b}_1 = 2 \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

$\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \bar{a}_2 = 2 \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} \text{ and } \bar{b}_2 = 3 \hat{i} - 5 \hat{j} + 2 \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} - \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) \times (3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -5 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 3 \hat{i} - \hat{j} - 7 \hat{k} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So $|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = \sqrt{9 + 1 + 49} = \sqrt{59}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the shortest distance between the given lines is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$d = \left| \frac{(\bar{\mathbf{b}}_1 \times \bar{\mathbf{b}}_2) \cdot (\bar{\mathbf{a}}_2 - \bar{\mathbf{a}}_1)}{|\bar{\mathbf{b}}_1 \times \bar{\mathbf{b}}_2|} \right| = \frac{|3 - 0 + 7|}{\sqrt{59}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{59}}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 Find the distance between the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ given by

$$\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2 \hat{j} - 4 \hat{k} + \lambda ( 2 \hat{i} + 3 \hat{j} + 6 \hat{k} )$$

and $$\vec{r} = 3 \hat{i} + 3 \hat{j} - 5 \hat{k} + \mu ( 2 \hat{i} + 3 \hat{j} + 6 \hat{k} )$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution The two lines are parallel (Why? ) We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the distance between the lines is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ d = \left| \frac{\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}|} \right| = \left| \frac{\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}}{\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36}} \right| $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $$= \frac{|-9\hat{i} + 14\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}|}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{293}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{293}}{7}$$

blocks.text:
Summary

Direction cosines of a line are the cosines of the angles made by the line
with the positive directions of the coordinate axes.
If $l, m, n$ are the direction cosines of a line, then $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.
Direction cosines of a line joining two points $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are

$$\frac{x_2 - x_1}{PQ}, \frac{y_2 - y_1}{PQ}, \frac{z_2 - z_1}{PQ}$$

where $PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$
Direction ratios of a line are the numbers which are proportional to the
direction cosines of a line.
If $l, m, n$ are the direction cosines and $a, b, c$ are the direction ratios of a line
then

$$l = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} ; m = \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} ; n = \frac{c}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$

Skew lines are lines in space which are neither parallel nor intersecting.
They lie in different planes.
Angle between skew lines is the angle between two intersecting lines
drawn from any point (preferably through the origin) parallel to each of the
skew lines.
If $l_1, m_1, n_1$ and $l_2, m_2, n_2$ are the direction cosines of two lines; and $\theta$ is the
acute angle between the two lines; then

$$\cos \theta = |l_1 l_2 + m_1 m_2 + n_1 n_2|$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
If $a_1$, $b_1$, $c_1$ and $a_2$, $b_2$, $c_2$ are the direction ratios of two lines and $\theta$ is the
acute angle between the two lines; then
$$\cos \theta = \left| \frac{a_1 \ a_2 + b_1 \ b_2 + c_1 \ c_2}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2} \ \sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}} \right|$$
Vector equation of a line that passes through the given point whose position
vector is $\vec{a}$ and parallel to a given vector $\vec{b}$ is $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \ \vec{b} \cdot$
Equation of a line through a point $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and having direction cosines $l, m, n$ is
$$\frac{x - x_1}{l} = \frac{y - y_1}{m} = \frac{z - z_1}{n}$$
The vector equation of a line which passes through two points whose position
vectors are $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \ (\vec{b} - \vec{a})$.
If $\theta$ is the acute angle between $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \ \vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \lambda \ \vec{b}_2$, then
$$\cos \theta = \left| \frac{\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1| \ |\vec{b}_2||} \right|$$
If $\frac{x - x_1}{l_1} = \frac{y - y_1}{m_1} = \frac{z - z_1}{n_1}$ and $\frac{x - x_2}{l_2} = \frac{y - y_2}{m_2} = \frac{z - z_2}{n_2}$
are the equations of two lines, then the acute angle between the two lines is
given by $\cos \theta = |l_1 l_2 + m_1 m_2 + n_1 n_2|$.
Shortest distance between two skew lines is the line segment perpendicular
to both the lines.
Shortest distance between $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \ \vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \ \vec{b}_2$ is
$$\left| \frac{(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|} \right|$$
Shortest distance between the lines: $\frac{x - x_1}{a_1} = \frac{y - y_1}{b_1} = \frac{z - z_1}{c_1}$ and
$$\frac{x - x_2}{a_2} = \frac{y - y_2}{b_2} = \frac{z - z_2}{c_2} \text{ is}$$
